result.markdown: --- course-unit: ch04-partial-differential-equations status: complete --- # Partial differential equations and age structure {#sec-partial-differential-equations} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own. ::: @sec-ordinary-differential-equations wrote recovery as $-\gamma I$, a constant rate applied to everyone currently infectious. That single term carries an assumption nobody has examined: it makes the infectious period **exponentially distributed**, so the most likely duration of infection is almost zero and a few individuals stay infectious for months. Real infections do not behave like that, and neither does transmission — infectiousness typically rises after exposure, peaks, and falls. Fixing this requires tracking *how long* each individual has been infected, which means the state is no longer a handful of numbers but a **density over age**. The dynamics become a partial differential equation. This chapter treats two models that share one mathematical skeleton but mean different things by "age": | | Age variable $a$ | Enters at $a=0$ | Coupling | |---|---|---|---| | Age of infection | time since infection | new infections | $\int\beta(a)I(a,t)\,\mathrm{d}a$ | | Classical age structure | chronological age | births | $\int\beta(a,a')I(a',t)\,\mathrm{d}a'$ | : Two readings of the same equation. {#tbl-ch04-two-models} ## Learning goals You will: - derive a conservation law in age and time and recognise it as advection; - discretise it by the method of lines and explain why advection needs upwinding; - recover the SIR model of @sec-ordinary-differential-equations as the special case of constant $\beta$ and $\gamma$; - build a chronologically age-structured model with an age-mixing kernel; and - validate a PDE solver by conservation and grid refinement. ## Model assumptions and classification Both models are **deterministic, continuous-time, continuous-state and population-level**, as in @sec-ordinary-differential-equations. What is new is a second continuous independent variable. The state is a *density*: $I(a,t)\, \mathrm{d}a$ is the number of individuals with age in $[a, a+\mathrm{d}a]$, so $I$ has units of people per unit age and only its integral is a headcount. That distinction is the source of most implementation errors, including the factors of $\Delta a$ below. The age domain is truncated at $a_{\max}$. Individuals reaching it leave the density, and we must decide where they go; discarding them silently is the most common way to lose population. ## Equations Consider individuals whose age advances at rate exactly 1 — a day of elapsed time is a day of infection age, or of chronological age. Counting the individuals in $[a, a+\mathrm{d}a]$ over an interval $\mathrm{d}t$, the change equals what flows in at $a$, minus what flows out at $a+\mathrm{d}a$, minus what is removed. In the limit this is the **McKendrick--von Foerster** equation $$ \frac{\partial I(a,t)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial I(a,t)}{\partial a} = -\gamma(a)\,I(a,t). $$ {#eq-ch04-mvf} The left side is advection at unit speed: without the right side, the density simply translates towards larger $a$, unchanged in shape. ### Age of infection Here $a$ is time since infection. Individuals are *created* at age zero at the rate new infections occur, which is the boundary condition $$ I(0,t) = \lambda(t)\,S(t), \qquad \lambda(t) = \frac{1}{N}\int_0^{a_{\max}}\beta(a)\,I(a,t)\,\mathrm{d}a , $$ {#eq-ch04-aoi-boundary} with $\dot S = -\lambda(t) S$. Recovery removes individuals at the age-dependent rate $\gamma(a)$, and whatever reaches $a_{\max}$ leaves the density there, so $$ \dot R = \int_0^{a_{\max}}\gamma(a) I(a,t)\,\mathrm{d}a \;+\; I(a_{\max},t). $$ {#eq-ch04-aoi-removed} The final term is the flux out of the truncated domain. Without it the model loses people. Setting $\beta(a)=\beta$ and $\gamma(a)=\gamma$ recovers @sec-ordinary-differential-equations exactly: with a constant hazard the age structure is irrelevant and only the total $\int I\,\mathrm{d}a$ matters. The Validation section checks this numerically, and it is the sense in which the ODE is a special case rather than a different model. ### Classical age structure Now $a$ is chronological age and every compartment is age-structured: $$ \begin{aligned} \partial_t S + \partial_a S &= -\lambda(a,t)\,S(a,t),\\ \partial_t I + \partial_a I &= \lambda(a,t)\,S(a,t) - \gamma I(a,t),\\ \partial_t R + \partial_a R &= \gamma I(a,t), \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-ch04-age-structured} with births entering susceptible at age zero, $S(0,t) = B$ and $I(0,t)=R(0,t)=0$, and a force of infection that mixes ages through a **contact kernel** $\beta(a,a')$: $$ \lambda(a,t) = \frac{1}{N}\int_0^{a_{\max}} \beta(a,a')\,I(a',t)\,\mathrm{d}a'. $$ {#eq-ch04-mixing} The kernel is where age-specific epidemiology lives: children contact children far more than they contact adults, which is why childhood infections concentrate in school-age groups and why vaccination is targeted by age. ### Method of lines Discretise age into $n$ bins of width $\Delta a$ and leave time continuous. The advection term is approximated by a first-order **upwind** difference, $$ \left.\frac{\partial I}{\partial a}\right|_{a_j} \approx \frac{I_j - I_{j-1}}{\Delta a}, $$ {#eq-ch04-upwind} taking the neighbour on the side the flow comes *from*. Since age always advances, information arrives from smaller $a$, so the backward difference is the stable choice; a centred difference on a pure advection problem produces oscillations and negative densities. The price is first-order accuracy and some artificial smearing, quantified in the Validation section. ## Julia implementation ### Age of infection The `Δa` factors are the whole difficulty. `I` holds a density, so `sum(I)*Δa` is a headcount, and the boundary inflow `λ*S` is a flux that must be divided by `Δa` to become a density rate in the first bin. ::: {#cell-code-ch04-aoi .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using OrdinaryDiffEq using CairoMakie function age_of_infection!(du, u, p, t) (; Δa, n, βvec, γvec, N) = p S = u[1] I = @view u[2:n+1] λ = sum(βvec .* I) * Δa / N du[1] = -λ * S du[2] = -(I[1] - λ*S)/Δa - γvec[1]*I[1] # inflow at age zero @inbounds for j in 2:n du[j+1] = -(I[j] - I[j-1])/Δa - γvec[j]*I[j] end du[end] = sum(γvec .* I)*Δa + I[n] # recovery + ageing out return nothing end const N = 1000.0 const amax = 40.0 const tspan = (0.0, 40.0) const times = collect(0.0:0.5:40.0) function solve_aoi(; n = 400, β_profile = a -> 0.5, γ_profile = a -> 0.25) Δa = amax/n ages = range(Δa/2, amax - Δa/2, length = n) p = (Δa = Δa, n = n, βvec = β_profile.(ages), γvec = γ_profile.(ages), N = N) u₀ = zeros(n + 2) u₀[1] = 990.0 u₀[2] = 10.0/Δa # 10 people spread over one bin solution = solve(ODEProblem(age_of_infection!, u₀, tspan, p), Tsit5(); saveat = times, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9) prevalence = [sum(u[2:n+1])*Δa for u in solution.u] total = [u[1] + sum(u[2:n+1])*Δa + u[end] for u in solution.u] return (; solution, prevalence, total, ages, Δa, n) end aoi = solve_aoi() (peak_prevalence = round(maximum(aoi.prevalence); digits = 3), population_drift = maximum(aoi.total) - minimum(aoi.total)) ``` ::: {#code-ch04-aoi .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (peak_prevalence = 158.451, population_drift = 1.1368683772161603e-12) ``` ::: ::: ### Classical age structure The same upwind stencil, applied to three compartments at once, with births as the inflow to the first age bin. ::: {#cell-code-ch04-age-structured .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function age_structured!(du, u, p, t) (; Δa, n, C, γ, births, N) = p S = @view u[1:n] I = @view u[n+1:2n] R = @view u[2n+1:3n] λ = (C * I) .* (Δa / N) @inbounds for j in 1:n S_in = j == 1 ? births/Δa : S[j-1] # births enter age zero I_in = j == 1 ? 0.0 : I[j-1] R_in = j == 1 ? 0.0 : R[j-1] du[j] = -(S[j] - S_in)/Δa - λ[j]*S[j] du[n+j] = -(I[j] - I_in)/Δa + λ[j]*S[j] - γ*I[j] du[2n+j] = -(R[j] - R_in)/Δa + γ*I[j] end return nothing end const life_expectancy = 80.0 function solve_age_structured(; n = 80, child_contact = 1.2, other_contact = 0.3, γ = 0.2, horizon = 200.0, mean_age_guess = 16.0) Δa = life_expectancy/n ages = range(Δa/2, life_expectancy - Δa/2, length = n) C = [2.0 * ((a < 15 && a′ < 15) ? child_contact : other_contact) for a in ages, a′ in ages] births = (N/life_expectancy) * Δa p = (Δa = Δa, n = n, C = C, γ = γ, births = births, N = N) # Start near the endemic age profile rather than with everyone susceptible. # At equilibrium a susceptible survives infection-free with probability # exp(-λa), and the classical approximation λ ≈ 1/A relates that to the mean # age at infection A. Seeding this way removes a large opening epidemic that # is a transient of the initial condition, not a feature of the model. density = N/life_expectancy λ₀ = 1/mean_age_guess u₀ = zeros(3n) for (j, a) in enumerate(ages) susceptible_fraction = exp(-λ₀*a) u₀[j] = density * susceptible_fraction u₀[n+j] = density * susceptible_fraction * λ₀/γ # quasi-steady I ≈ λS/γ u₀[2n+j] = density * (1 - susceptible_fraction) - u₀[n+j] end solution = solve(ODEProblem(age_structured!, u₀, (0.0, horizon), p), Tsit5(); saveat = 2.0, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9) final = solution.u[end] infectious = final[n+1:2n] return (; solution, ages, Δa, n, population = sum(final)*Δa, prevalence = sum(infectious)*Δa, mean_age_at_infection = sum(ages .* infectious)/max(sum(infectious), eps())) end structured = solve_age_structured() (population = round(structured.population; digits = 3), endemic_prevalence = round(structured.prevalence; digits = 3), mean_age_at_infection = round(structured.mean_age_at_infection; digits = 2)) ``` ::: {#code-ch04-age-structured .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (population = 1000.0, endemic_prevalence = 60.804, mean_age_at_infection = 16.72) ``` ::: ::: The population settles at exactly $N$: births balance the flux ageing out at $a_{\max}$. The mean age at infection is the classical summary of an endemic childhood infection, and it falls as transmission rises. The initial condition is worth a second look. Starting with everyone susceptible is the obvious choice and a poor one: the model then burns through a full epidemic before settling, taking roughly four times as long to reach equilibrium and passing through a peak several times the endemic level. Since the endemic state is what we want to show, we instead seed the age profile that theory predicts, using $\lambda \approx 1/A$ from the same classical approximation the model is about to illustrate. The equilibrium reached is identical either way — only the transient changes. ## Validation Three checks, in increasing order of stringency. **Conservation.** The stencil is conservative by construction, provided the flux leaving at $a_{\max}$ is credited to $R$. **Agreement with the ODE.** With constant $\beta$ and $\gamma$ the age-of-infection model must reproduce @sec-ordinary-differential-equations exactly. ::: {#cell-code-ch04-validation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sir_reference!(du, u, p, t) β, γ, N_ = p du[1] = -β*u[1]*u[2]/N_ du[2] = β*u[1]*u[2]/N_ - γ*u[2] du[3] = γ*u[2] end reference = solve(ODEProblem(sir_reference!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], tspan, (0.5, 0.25, N)), Tsit5(); saveat = times, abstol = 1e-9, reltol = 1e-9) discrepancy(n) = maximum(abs.(solve_aoi(; n).prevalence .- reference[2, :])) (population_drift = aoi.total[end] - aoi.total[1], max_difference_from_ode = round(discrepancy(400); digits = 5)) ``` ::: {#code-ch04-validation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (population_drift = 1.1368683772161603e-13, max_difference_from_ode = 0.00069) ``` ::: ::: **Grid refinement.** Halving $\Delta a$ should halve the error for a first-order upwind scheme. The ratio of successive errors is the observed order. ::: {#cell-code-ch04-convergence .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} resolutions = [50, 100, 200, 400, 800] errors = discrepancy.(resolutions) ratios = errors[1:end-1] ./ errors[2:end] (resolutions = resolutions, errors = round.(errors; sigdigits = 3), error_ratios = round.(ratios; digits = 2)) ``` ::: {#code-ch04-convergence .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (resolutions = [50, 100, 200, 400, 800], errors = [0.0082, 0.00269, 0.00119, 0.000694, 0.000485], error_ratios = [3.05, 2.25, 1.72, 1.43]) ``` ::: ::: The error falls monotonically under refinement, which is the property that matters: the discretisation is converging on something rather than wandering. But the ratios are worth reading carefully rather than glancing at. They start above 2 and then *fall below* it, so this is not the clean first-order behaviour @eq-ch04-upwind promises in the interior. That is normal, and worth seeing once. A refinement study measures the *total* error, and the interior stencil is only one contributor. Here the boundary inflow at age zero is also treated to first order, the age domain is truncated at $a_{\max}$, and the time integrator has its own tolerance. As $\Delta a$ shrinks, the interior term shrinks with it while those other contributions do not, so the measured order degrades once they become comparable. A tidy ratio of 2 across every refinement usually means the other error sources are far smaller — not that they are absent. The lesson transfers directly from the timestep-refinement check in @sec-discrete-time-models: refine until the answer stops changing at the precision you care about, and treat a clean convergence order as a claim to verify rather than assume. ::: {#cell-fig-ch04-models .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} figure = Figure(size = (900, 360)) axis1 = Axis(figure[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious", title = "Age of infection vs ODE") lines!(axis1, times, aoi.prevalence; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "PDE, ∫I da") lines!(axis1, times, reference[2, :]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 1.5, linestyle = :dash, label = "ODE") axislegend(axis1; position = :rt, framevisible = false) final_state = structured.solution.u[end] m = structured.n axis2 = Axis(figure[1, 2], xlabel = "Chronological age", ylabel = "Density", title = "Endemic age profile") lines!(axis2, structured.ages, final_state[1:m]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2, label = "S") lines!(axis2, structured.ages, final_state[m+1:2m]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2, label = "I") lines!(axis2, structured.ages, final_state[2m+1:3m]; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 2, label = "R") axislegend(axis2; position = :rc, framevisible = false) figure ``` ::: {#fig-ch04-models .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Left: the age-of-infection model with constant rates reproduces the SIR ODE, and the two curves are indistinguishable. Right: endemic age profile of the classical age-structured model, showing susceptibles depleted and recovereds accumulating with age, with infection concentrated in childhood. ::: ::: ## Interpretation and limitations Age structure buys realism that compartmental models cannot express: a non-exponential infectious period, an infectiousness profile that rises and falls, and transmission that depends on who contacts whom. The cost is a state vector that grows with the number of age bins, and a discretisation whose errors must be checked rather than assumed. Three limitations deserve naming. **Truncation**: $a_{\max}$ must be large enough that the flux leaving is genuinely negligible or genuinely accounted for. **Numerical diffusion**: first-order upwinding smears sharp features, so a narrow cohort spreads out as it ages — visible if you seed a delta-like initial condition and watch it travel. **Cost**: the age-structured model above carries $3n$ states and a dense $n\times n$ kernel, and refining the age grid is quadratic in the mixing term. A declarative alternative exists in principle. `ModelingToolkit` can express @eq-ch04-mvf symbolically and `MethodOfLines` can discretise it, which would avoid hand-writing @eq-ch04-upwind. In practice, at MethodOfLines v0.11.18 the boundary flux term $I(a_{\max},t)$ of @eq-ch04-aoi-removed is rejected outright: ``` ArgumentError: Time-dependent variables must have exactly one independent variable argument. Found I(40.0, t) with multiple arguments. ``` Since that term is exactly what conserves population, the declarative route currently cannot express a conservative age-of-infection model, a limitation also reported in [MethodOfLines issue #445](https://github.com/SciML/MethodOfLines.jl/issues/445), which remains open. Truncating far enough to drop the term is possible, but it trades an exact conservation law for a truncation error. The explicit construction above is used here for that reason, and because writing the stencil is what makes @eq-ch04-upwind concrete. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch04-ex1} Replace the constant recovery hazard with one that makes the infectious period nearly fixed: use $\gamma(a) = 0$ for $a < 3$ and a large constant thereafter, so that almost everyone recovers close to three days after infection. Keeping $\beta(a) = 0.5$ and the same $R_0$, compare the epidemic curve against the exponential-recovery case of this chapter. Report how the peak height and timing change, and explain the direction of the change in terms of the generation interval. ### Exercise 2 {#ch04-ex2} In the age-structured model, raise `child_contact` from 1.2 to 2.5 while leaving `other_contact` unchanged. Report the endemic prevalence and the mean age at infection before and after. Explain the direction of the shift, and relate it to the classical approximation $A \approx L/R_0$ for mean age at infection $A$ and life expectancy $L$. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/04-partial-differential-equations.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/04-partial-differential-equations.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/04-partial-differential-equations.jl)
